title: Arithmetic mod n
short: Reduce first, then add, subtract and multiply: the result is the same as reducing at the end.
trouble: Students cancel a common factor from both sides of a congruence: 2 · 3 ≡ 2 · 1 (mod 4), yet 3 ≢ 1 (mod 4).

blocks.html: The point of congruences is that you can calculate with them almost like equations. Adding, subtracting and multiplying all respect congruence, so you may replace any number by anything congruent to it, usually something small, before you compute.

Theorem. If $a \equiv a'$ and $b \equiv b' \pmod{n}$, then $$a + b \equiv a' + b', \qquad a - b \equiv a' - b', \qquad ab \equiv a'b' \pmod{n}.$$ Applying the last rule again and again, $a^{k} \equiv (a')^{k}$ for every $k \ge 1$.

Sums and differences: $(a + b) - (a' + b') = (a - a') + (b - b')$ is a sum of two multiples of $n$. Products take one trick, adding and subtracting $ab'$: $$ab - a'b' = a(b - b') + b'(a - a').$$ Both terms are multiples of $n$, so the difference is too.

blocks.text: What you may not do: cancel freely

blocks.html: Division is different. $2 \cdot 3 \equiv 2 \cdot 1 \pmod{4}$ (both sides are $\equiv 2$), yet $3 \not\equiv 1 \pmod{4}$. Cancelling the $2$ fails because $2$ shares a factor with the modulus $4$. The picture shows why: multiplying by $2$ mod $4$ sends both $1$ and $3$ to the same place, so you cannot tell afterward where you started.

blocks.name: nt-clock
blocks.cap: Arrows from each $x$ to $2x \bmod 4$: $1$ and $3$ both land on $2$, and $0$ and $2$ both land on $0$. Multiplying by 2 loses information, so it cannot be undone. Try $a = 3$: then every point is hit exactly once.

blocks.html: The rule that does hold: if $ca \equiv cb \pmod{n}$ and $\gcd(c, n) = 1$, then $a \equiv b \pmod{n}$. (Here $n \mid c(a - b)$ with no common factor in $c$, so $n \mid (a - b)$.) In general you may only conclude $a \equiv b \pmod{n/\gcd(c, n)}$. Modular inverses make this precise.

head: $\times$
blocks.cap: Multiplication mod 6. The rows of 2, 3 and 4 repeat values and never reach 1, and $2 \cdot 3 \equiv 0$ although neither factor is 0. The rows of 1 and 5 contain every residue once.

blocks.html: Cancelling a common factor from both sides of a congruence. From $2 \cdot 3 \equiv 2 \cdot 1 \pmod{4}$ you cannot conclude $3 \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$. Check $\gcd(c, n)$ before cancelling $c$: cancel only when it is $1$, and otherwise divide the modulus by the gcd too.
Add, subtract and multiply mod $n$ freely, reducing whenever you like: the answer is the same as reducing at the end. Cancel a factor only when it is coprime to $n$.
